title: From Death to Life, from Strangers to Family
summary: God saves the spiritually dead by grace through faith, creates them for good works, and reconciles Jews and Gentiles in one body, household, and Spirit-filled temple.
literaryContext: The resurrection power celebrated at the end of chapter 1 is applied first to humanity’s passage from death to life and then to the corporate reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles. Both movements begin with divine grace and end with a new creation shaped for holiness, unity, and God’s indwelling presence.

outline.title: Made Alive by Grace
outline.summary: God raises sinners from spiritual death with Christ; salvation is His gift received through faith and produces a new walk in good works.

outline.title: Those Far Off Brought Near
outline.summary: Gentiles once separated from covenant hope are brought near to God and His people through the blood of Christ.

outline.title: Christ Is Our Peace
outline.summary: Through the cross Christ removes hostility, creates one new humanity, and gives Jews and Gentiles shared access to the Father in one Spirit.

outline.title: One Household and Temple
outline.summary: Former strangers become citizens, family members, and living stones in the Spirit-filled dwelling God builds upon Christ and the apostolic witness.

verses.bibleText: And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The opening words carry the thought of Ephesians 1:19–23 into the experience of believers. Paul has just described the power by which God raised Christ from the dead and exalted Him above every hostile authority. He now explains what that same resurrection power accomplished in people who believed the gospel.

The words “hath he quickened” are supplied by the KJV to complete the thought. In Greek, Paul begins, “And you, being dead,” then delays the main verb until verse 5. The suspended sentence allows the darkness of the former condition to gather weight before God’s life-giving action is announced.

Death here is not physical inactivity. Verse 2 describes these same people as walking, choosing, and disobeying. They were physically alive but separated from the life of God, unable to produce spiritual life from within themselves, and living beneath the sentence that sin ultimately brings. Their condition was both relational and moral: alienated from God, governed by sin, and travelling toward death.

“Trespasses and sins” identifies the cause and sphere of this death. Human beings have not merely suffered misfortune; they have violated God’s will. Yet the verse offers hope through its past tense: “ye were dead.” The gospel does not improve spiritual corpses by education or discipline. God gives life where life is absent. The same Christ who rose bodily from the grave becomes the source of present spiritual life and the guarantee of bodily resurrection when He returns.

wordNotes.explanation: The word describes existence under the power and sentence of death because of sin. In this context it refers particularly to spiritual alienation from God, though it also points toward the physical and final death that sin brings.

wordNotes.term: trespasses and sins — παραπτώμασιν καὶ ἁμαρτίαις (paraptōmasin kai hamartiais)
wordNotes.explanation: The two terms together give a comprehensive description of human rebellion. Trespasses are violations or false steps; sins are acts and conditions that fall short of God’s will. Paul’s emphasis lies on the completeness of the sinful condition rather than on a strict distinction between the words.

verses.bibleText: Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Spiritual death was not motionless. Those who were dead toward God nevertheless “walked” continually in sin. The image describes a settled direction rather than an occasional failure. Sin formed the road, the surrounding atmosphere, and the habitual pattern of their lives.

Three influences emerge across verses 2–3: the world, the devil, and the flesh. “The course of this world” is the present order organized in rebellion against God. It includes values, customs, ambitions, and systems that make unbelief appear normal and obedience appear foolish. The world’s course changes outwardly from age to age, but its inward direction remains self-exaltation and resistance to its Creator.

Behind that visible order stands “the prince of the power of the air.” Paul speaks of a real personal enemy who presides over hostile spiritual powers. People in Ephesus and the wider Roman world often feared unseen forces and attempted to manipulate them through magic. The gospel announces something far greater than protection through charms: Christ has been exalted far above every principality and power, and those who belong to Him share in His victory.

Satan’s influence is described as a spirit now working in “the children of disobedience.” The phrase identifies people by their controlling disposition. Their disobedience includes both refusal to trust God and refusal to submit to His will. Satan does not remove human responsibility; he works through desires, beliefs, and choices that people willingly embrace.

This diagnosis prevents shallow views of evil. Sin is personal, social, and spiritual. Human beings cannot excuse themselves by blaming society or the devil, but neither should they underestimate the forces encouraging rebellion. Deliverance requires more than improved surroundings. It requires transfer into Christ’s kingdom, renewal by the Spirit, and a new walk shaped by the will of God.

wordNotes.explanation: Walking is a biblical image for one’s settled manner of life. The former life of the readers was conducted within sin and shaped by forces opposed to God.

wordNotes.term: prince of the power of the air — ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος (archonta tēs exousias tou aeros)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression refers to Satan as ruler over the rebellious spiritual powers. The language of the air reflects an ancient way of describing the invisible realm surrounding earthly life; it is not a scientific description of the atmosphere.

verses.bibleText: Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The circle now widens from “ye” to “we all.” Paul refuses to describe the Gentile past as though Jewish birth, religious knowledge, or apostolic office placed him outside humanity’s common need. Every believer has a former life from which grace has rescued him. No ethnic or religious group possesses a naturally righteous standing before God.

The KJV expression “had our conversation” refers to conduct. Paul and his readers formerly lived under the rule of disordered desires. “Flesh” does not mean that the physical body is inherently evil. Scripture treats the body as God’s creation and as destined for resurrection. Here the flesh is human nature functioning independently of God—self-centred, weakened by the fall, and inclined toward rebellion.

Sin is not confined to bodily appetite. Paul adds “the desires of the flesh and of the mind.” Thought, imagination, judgment, and intention may become as rebellious as physical passion. Some sins are impulsive; others are carefully reasoned. The whole person needs renewal.

“By nature the children of wrath” describes the grave result. Humanity enters life within Adam’s fallen order, possessing weakness and inclination toward sin, and then confirms that condition through personal transgression. The wording does not portray God as arbitrarily hating human beings or assigning guilt without moral reality. His wrath is His holy and settled opposition to evil—the response of righteous love to everything that destroys His creatures and contradicts His character.

Wrath must not be confused with uncontrolled temper. God’s judgment is truthful, proportionate, and directed toward the final removal of unrepented sin. Those who persist in rebellion remain under that judgment; they do not possess an immortal life that can continue endlessly apart from God. Sin ends in death.

The phrase “even as others” removes every ground for superiority. Jew and Gentile, religious and irreligious, disciplined and openly immoral all need the same mercy. Yet Paul is describing the past of believers. Fallen nature is real, but it is not an irresistible destiny. God’s grace can liberate the will, renew the mind, and create a new life in Christ.

wordNotes.explanation: In the KJV, conversation often means conduct or manner of life rather than speech. Paul includes himself and all believers among those who formerly lived within the rebellious order.

wordNotes.term: children of wrath by nature — τέκνα φύσει ὀργῆς (tekna physei orgēs)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes humanity’s fallen condition and its resulting exposure to God’s judgment. People inherit a nature inclined toward sin and then personally express that condition through sinful desires and choices.

verses.bibleText: But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Two words turn the entire passage: “But God.” Nothing in verses 1–3 suggests that humanity could reverse its condition. Sin had affected conduct, desire, thought, relationships, and destiny. The saving change therefore begins outside the sinner, in the character and action of God.

God is “rich in mercy.” Mercy is His compassionate response to the miserable and guilty. Its richness means that human need cannot exhaust it and human unworthiness does not prevent Him from acting. This mercy is not reluctance to uphold justice. At the cross, God confronted sin with complete seriousness while providing forgiveness for sinners.

The fountain of mercy is “his great love wherewith he loved us.” Paul does not locate the reason for salvation in human attractiveness, spiritual promise, or future usefulness. God loved those who were dead, disobedient, and deserving of judgment. His love is therefore sovereign in initiative and restorative in purpose.

Wrath in verse 3 and love in verse 4 are not contradictory descriptions of God. Holy love opposes what destroys its object. God’s wrath declares that evil matters; His mercy provides the way by which sinners may be delivered from evil without justice being denied.

The verse also prepares for Christian ethics. Those who live because of rich mercy cannot treat others with cold severity. The grace received from God becomes the pattern for patience, forgiveness, generosity, and compassionate action. Believers show that they understand divine mercy when they extend mercy without turning truth into indifference.

verses.bibleText: Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God acted at the very point of human helplessness: “even when we were dead in sins.” He did not wait for spiritual life to appear before giving life. Repentance, faith, and obedience become possible because grace awakens, calls, and enables the sinner; they are not qualities by which the sinner first persuades God to be merciful.

To be “quickened together with Christ” is to be made alive in union with the risen Lord. Christ’s resurrection was bodily, historical, and victorious. The believer’s present quickening is spiritual and relational: alienation gives way to reconciliation, bondage to a new freedom, and deathward existence to communion with God.

This present life does not replace the future bodily resurrection. Believers still suffer, age, and die, and Scripture locates their physical resurrection at Christ’s return. The life already received is the beginning and pledge of what will then be completed. The risen Christ who now lives in His people will raise their mortal bodies in the last day.

The interruption “by grace ye are saved” reveals Paul’s amazement. Grace is not merely divine assistance added to human achievement. It is God’s undeserved action for those who could not rescue themselves. Christ is the ground of salvation; grace is its source; faith, as verse 8 will explain, is the means by which it is received.

The perfect construction translated “ye are saved” stresses a present state produced by God’s past action. Believers may know that they have passed from death unto life and need not live under continual uncertainty about God’s willingness to receive them. Yet salvation must continue to be embraced through living faith. The same letter that announces present salvation later calls believers to walk worthily, resist evil, and stand in the armour of God. Assurance rests in Christ, not in a presumption that continuing unbelief or deliberate rebellion can never separate a person from Him.

wordNotes.term: quickened us together with Christ — συνεζωοποίησεν τῷ Χριστῷ (synezōopoiēsen tō Christō)
wordNotes.explanation: God made believers alive in union with the risen Christ. The compound verb emphasizes participation with Christ: His resurrection life becomes the source of their new spiritual existence.

wordNotes.term: by grace ye are saved — χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι (chariti este sesōsmenoi)
wordNotes.explanation: The construction emphasizes a saving act whose effects continue in the present. Grace is placed first for emphasis: salvation originates entirely in God’s undeserved favour.

verses.bibleText: And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Union with Christ reaches from new life to resurrection and enthronement. Three actions belong together: God made believers alive with Christ, raised them with Him, and seated them with Him in the heavenly places. The repetition of “together” emphasizes that no saving benefit exists independently of the Saviour.

Christ was literally raised from death and enthroned at God’s right hand. Believers share these realities in Him. Their old allegiance has been broken, their citizenship has changed, and their representative Head now reigns above every hostile power. What is true of Him determines the standing and destiny of His people.

Their bodies remain mortal, and the resurrection of the righteous still awaits Christ’s return. Paul is therefore describing a present spiritual and covenantal participation, not the transportation of conscious souls to heavenly thrones. The future is so secure in the risen Christ that its reality can be spoken of as already begun.

This position directly answers the fear created by verse 2. The prince of the power of the air is not above the believer’s Lord. Christ reigns far above him, and believers are joined to that victorious Christ. Spiritual conflict continues—Ephesians 6 makes that plain—but Christians fight from belonging to the Victor, not in the hope of creating a victory the cross and resurrection failed to achieve.

Being seated with Christ does not authorize pride or domination. The One enthroned is the crucified Lord whose power is revealed in self-giving love. Participation in His reign means freedom to serve, courage to resist evil, and confidence that no earthly or demonic authority can nullify God’s purpose.

The phrase “in Christ Jesus” governs the whole promise. There is no exalted status attached to ancestry, office, knowledge, or religious performance. Everything depends on continuing relationship with Christ. Apart from Him humanity remains under the course of this world; in Him believers possess life, victory, and the assured hope of resurrection glory.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb depicts believers as sharing Christ’s resurrection victory through union with Him. Their spiritual resurrection is already real, while their bodily resurrection remains future.
Believers share covenantally and representatively in Christ’s exalted position. Christ alone sits at the Father’s right hand, but those who are in Him participate in His victory and security.

verses.bibleText: That in the ages to come he might shew the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God’s saving work has an eternal purpose: to display “the exceeding riches of his grace.” The redeemed are not merely rescued from danger and then forgotten. Through every coming age, God continues to reveal the depth of His kindness toward them in Christ.

The plural “ages to come” carries the mind beyond the present order toward the consummation of salvation and the life of the new creation. Paul does not provide a detailed chronology here. His point is that no future age will outgrow grace. The redeemed will never look back and conclude that they owe their life to their own merit.

God’s kindness is concrete grace. It appears in forgiveness, adoption, spiritual life, victory over hostile powers, resurrection, and final fellowship with Him. Each gift arises “through Christ Jesus.” Eternity will not move beyond Christ as though the cross were an introductory lesson. The Lamb who redeemed His people remains the everlasting revelation of God’s character.

The verse also gives salvation a cosmic dimension. The transformation of rebels into holy and loving children demonstrates that God’s government is both just and gracious. The history of redemption will bear lasting witness that He neither excused evil nor abandoned sinners. At immeasurable cost, He overcame evil through Christ and recreated those who trusted Him.

Grace therefore has a public fruit in the present. When believers forgive, serve, reconcile, and live in holiness, they begin to display the divine kindness that eternity will more fully reveal. A church marked by pride and cruelty obscures the purpose for which it has been saved; a community transformed by grace makes God’s character visible.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to demonstrate or provide visible evidence of something. God’s treatment of the redeemed displays the character and abundance of His grace.

verses.bibleText: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Grace now receives its fullest explanation. “By grace” identifies the source of salvation: God’s undeserved favour and effective action. “Through faith” identifies the means of reception. Neither phrase allows the sinner to claim credit.

Grace is more than a favourable attitude in God. It is the mercy that made the dead alive, raised them with Christ, and placed them within His victory. Salvation includes pardon, reconciliation, new life, deliverance from hostile powers, and the hope of resurrection. Its whole movement begins with God.

Faith is not a competing contribution supplied by humanity. It does not possess merit equal to Christ’s obedience, nor does it persuade an unwilling God to be gracious. Faith abandons self-reliance and rests in the sufficiency of Christ. It includes believing the gospel, trusting the Saviour, yielding to Him, and continuing in dependence upon His promise.

The words “and that not of yourselves” most naturally refer to the entire preceding statement—salvation by grace through faith. The grammatical gender of “that” does not correspond directly to either “grace” or “faith,” and verse 9 continues by denying that the same saving reality comes from works. Paul’s central concern is not to isolate one component but to remove salvation in its entirety from the realm of human boasting.

Calling salvation “the gift of God” does not make the human response unreal. A gift may be offered, resisted, neglected, or received. God does not believe in place of the sinner, but His grace awakens and enables a genuine response. Faith is therefore active without being meritorious and freely exercised without becoming self-salvation.

This balance protects assurance and responsibility. The believer’s confidence rests in Christ’s finished sacrifice and present saving power, not in the strength of personal emotion or the perfection of performance. Yet living faith does not remain a momentary opinion. It clings to Christ, receives the Spirit, and begins the new walk described in verse 10.

No ceremony, moral achievement, inherited privilege, church position, or human mediator can replace this relationship. Salvation is received through faith because only faith gives all glory to the One who gives the gift.

wordNotes.explanation: Faith is the means of receiving God’s saving gift. It is personal trust in God’s promise and commitment to Christ, not a meritorious achievement that earns grace.
The neuter pronoun most naturally points to the whole preceding reality—salvation by grace through faith—rather than to faith alone. The entire saving event is not humanly produced but is God’s gift.

verses.bibleText: Not of works, lest any man should boast.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Every ground of self-congratulation is removed. Salvation is “not of works,” because people who were dead in sin could not produce the life by which they were rescued. God’s gift cannot be converted into wages without destroying the meaning of grace.

The excluded works include every attempt to establish acceptance through religious, moral, ceremonial, or humanitarian achievement. Obedience to God is good, but obedience cannot erase earlier guilt, supply an atoning sacrifice, or give life to the spiritually dead. Even actions commanded by God become distorted when used as grounds of merit.

The purpose clause “lest any man should boast” exposes the inward attraction of works-righteousness. The sinful heart prefers a salvation that leaves room for comparison: one person appears more disciplined, enlightened, pure, or deserving than another. The cross silences that boasting. Before it, all stand as sinners and all who are saved receive the same mercy.

Grace also excludes ethnic and ecclesiastical boasting. Jewish covenant privilege could not justify, and Gentile inclusion did not create a new reason for arrogance. No denomination, congregation, office, or theological knowledge makes Christ indebted to its possessor.

Verse 10 prevents the words from being twisted into indifference toward conduct. Works do not cause salvation, but salvation creates a people devoted to good works. Deeds are fruit and evidence of living faith, never payment for grace. In the judgment, they reveal whether the professed relationship with Christ bore its promised fruit; they do not replace Christ as the sinner’s righteousness.

The only legitimate boast is in the Lord. The believer may rejoice, but the praise moves away from self toward the Father who planned salvation, the Son who accomplished it, and the Spirit who applies it.

wordNotes.term: not of works — οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων (ouk ex ergōn)
wordNotes.explanation: Works are excluded as the source or basis of salvation. Paul is not condemning obedient deeds themselves; he is denying that anything human beings perform can earn God’s saving verdict or place Him in their debt.

verses.bibleText: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The exclusion of works as the cause of salvation leads immediately to their inclusion as its purpose. “We are his workmanship.” God does not merely cancel a record and leave the sinner unchanged. He creates a new person in union with Christ.

The language recalls creation. The One who formed humanity at the beginning now performs a work of re-creation in people damaged by sin. The Christian therefore has no basis for spiritual pride. Whatever is genuinely holy in the life is evidence of the Creator’s workmanship.

“Created in Christ Jesus” identifies the sphere and agent of this new existence. Moral reform detached from Christ may alter habits without giving spiritual life. The gospel joins the believer to the crucified and risen Lord, from whom forgiveness, power, and a new identity flow.

Good works are the intended result. They include acts of love, justice, truthfulness, purity, generosity, reconciliation, faithful labour, and obedience to God’s revealed will. They do not purchase salvation; they express the life salvation has created. Paul’s sequence is decisive: saved by grace, not from works, created for good works.

God has “before ordained,” or prepared beforehand, this path. His eternal purpose was never merely to rescue people from punishment while leaving them devoted to the same rebellion. He chose a people to be holy and blameless, and through the Spirit He writes His will upon their hearts. Grace restores obedience to its proper place—as loving response rather than anxious payment.

The verb “walk” deliberately recalls verse 2. Believers once walked in trespasses according to the world’s course; now they are to walk in works prepared by God. Conversion changes direction. The Christian life is not sinless self-sufficiency, but it is a real new course marked by repentance, growth, and Spirit-enabled obedience.

Divine preparation does not make human participation unnecessary. Paul says that “we should walk” in these works. God supplies calling, opportunity, strength, and grace, while believers willingly cooperate with Him. Even the fruit gives no occasion for boasting, because both the new life and the path in which it moves come from God.

A profession of faith with no transforming fruit contradicts the purpose of new creation. Conversely, believers need not perform good works to manufacture an identity. They serve because they already are God’s workmanship, accepted in Christ and empowered to display His character.

wordNotes.explanation: The word means something made or created. Believers are the product of God’s re-creative action, not self-made spiritual achievements.
God has already purposed the kind of life His renewed people should live. The wording stresses divine initiative without eliminating the believer’s responsibility to walk in that prepared way.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A second call to remember begins the chapter’s corporate movement. Verses 1–10 recalled what all believers had been in sin; verses 11–22 focus on the particular alienation experienced by Gentiles. Memory is meant to deepen gratitude and destroy pride, not preserve humiliation.

Circumcision had been given to Abraham as a covenant sign and became a visible marker of Jewish identity. Gentiles were called “the Uncircumcision,” while Jews were known as “the Circumcision.” Such labels could carry contempt in both directions. Jews often regarded uncircumcised Gentiles as outside the covenant and morally unclean; Greeks and Romans frequently mocked Jewish circumcision.

Paul calls it circumcision “in the flesh made by hands.” He is not rewriting Israel’s history as though the sign had never come from God. He is showing that a physical operation cannot itself transform the heart or determine membership in the new community formed by Christ. What human hands perform outwardly cannot substitute for the inward renewal accomplished by the Spirit.

The phrase also prepares for the removal of the dividing barrier in verses 14–15. A sign intended to mark covenant identity had become, in sinful use, a badge of superiority and an instrument of separation. Christ did not resolve the conflict by requiring all Gentiles to become Jewish proselytes or by teaching Jews to despise their ancestry. He created a new humanity in which neither circumcision nor uncircumcision establishes spiritual rank.

“Remember” therefore carries two pastoral directions. Gentile believers must never forget that the gospel came to them through promises entrusted to Israel; gratitude leaves no room for anti-Jewish arrogance. Jewish believers must never use historical privilege to deny full fellowship to those whom Christ has received. Both groups stand before God through the same grace.

wordNotes.explanation: The term literally refers to the foreskin and became a designation for Gentiles. In this setting it reflects the social and religious distance—and sometimes contempt—between Jews and Gentiles.

The phrase stresses the external, physical character of circumcision. Paul does not deny its former covenantal significance, but he relativizes it in comparison with the inward work accomplished through Christ.

verses.bibleText: That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul gathers the Gentiles’ former condition into five closely related losses. Their deepest deprivation was not lack of civilisation, philosophy, or religious activity. It was separation from the saving revelation and covenant purpose of the true God.

They were first “without Christ.” Before hearing the gospel, they stood outside the Messiah and the blessings located in Him. Israel’s Scriptures nourished hope in the coming Anointed One; the nations generally lacked that revealed expectation. Now that the Messiah has come, the phrase also means that no saving life exists apart from personal union with Jesus.

They were “aliens from the commonwealth of Israel.” The word may include citizenship, corporate identity, privileges, and way of life. Israel had received God’s oracles, worship, covenant instruction, and messianic promises. These advantages did not make every Israelite righteous, but they were real gifts intended ultimately to bless all nations.

The Gentiles were also “strangers from the covenants of promise.” God’s covenants with Abraham and Israel traced the pathway of redemption, promising blessing, the Messiah, the Spirit, and a restored people. Gentiles were not naturally included in that covenant administration, though the promises always anticipated blessing reaching the nations.

Consequently they had “no hope.” Paul is describing an objective condition, not saying that every Gentile felt constant despair. Pagan society contained hopes of prosperity, fame, family continuity, and uncertain existence beyond death. It did not possess the biblical hope of forgiveness, resurrection, and everlasting life in God’s restored creation. Without God’s promise, death remained an undefeated enemy.

Finally, they were “without God in the world.” Ephesus was deeply religious, and its inhabitants honoured many supposed deities. Yet plurality of worship did not amount to knowledge of the Creator. Idolatry left people exposed to the very spiritual powers they hoped to appease.

The verse must not be used to cultivate contempt for Gentiles or to imply that God had no concern for nations before Christ. Scripture repeatedly shows Him seeking them, and every person who has ever been saved is saved through the grace ultimately revealed in Christ. Paul is describing the ordinary salvation-historical distance of the nations from the covenant revelation entrusted to Israel.

This fivefold loss makes verse 13 luminous. The gospel does more than improve religious understanding. It brings the Christless into Christ, strangers into covenant blessing, the hopeless into resurrection hope, and those without God into the household of the Father.

wordNotes.term: commonwealth of Israel — πολιτείας τοῦ Ἰσραήλ (politeias tou Israēl)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase may include Israel’s corporate life, citizenship, privileges, and covenant-shaped way of living. Gentiles ordinarily stood outside the community entrusted with God’s Scriptures and promises.
The word means without the true God, not necessarily without religious belief. The Gentile world contained many gods and cults, but its idolatry did not provide reconciled knowledge of the Creator.

verses.bibleText: But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Against that fivefold deprivation comes another decisive contrast: “But now.” The change is not produced by Gentiles moving themselves closer through moral improvement, cultural assimilation, or adoption of Jewish identity. It occurs “in Christ Jesus.”

Those once “far off” have been “made nigh.” Nearness includes reconciliation with God and incorporation into His covenant people. The Gentiles are not left at the edge of a Jewish community as tolerated visitors. They receive full access to the Father and full fellowship with all who belong to Christ.

The means is “the blood of Christ.” Blood signifies His genuine human life poured out in sacrificial death. Jesus did not reconcile humanity through teaching alone or by overlooking guilt. He gave Himself. His once-for-all sacrifice dealt with sin, fulfilled the meaning of the ancient sacrificial types, and opened the way into God’s presence.

The phrase does not attribute magical power to physical substance detached from Christ. It is a compact way of speaking about the obedient, self-giving death of the divine Son in human flesh. The One whose blood was shed is the risen Lord; the sacrifice is effective because of who He is and because the Father accepted His offering.

Nearness is therefore costly grace. Believers may approach God confidently, but never casually or boastfully. Every prayer and every act of fellowship rests upon a life given at the cross.

The verse also binds reconciliation with God to reconciliation among people. The same blood brings every believer near. No person may claim a closer saving distance because of ethnicity, ancestry, education, or religious history. Those who have been brought near by one sacrifice are summoned to receive one another as people standing on the same holy ground.

wordNotes.term: far off ... made nigh — μακρὰν ... ἐγγὺς (makran ... engys)
wordNotes.explanation: The language echoes Isaiah’s promise of peace to those far and near. Gentiles once distant from covenant privilege and fellowship with God have been brought into His presence and people through Christ.

verses.bibleText: For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peace is no longer merely a condition to be achieved; it is identified with a Person: “he is our peace.” Christ does not stand at a distance from two hostile groups and persuade each to compromise. He brings both into Himself, where an entirely new relationship is created.

Biblical peace carries the richness of wholeness, reconciliation, security, and restored fellowship. Here the cessation of hostility between Jew and Gentile is central. Their unity does not depend upon minimizing the past or pretending their differences were imaginary. It rests upon Christ’s work strong enough to overcome them.

“He hath made both one.” The two groups are not blended by Gentiles becoming Jews or Jews becoming Gentiles. Cultural histories may remain, but they no longer determine access to God, spiritual rank, or membership in His people. Both are redefined by relationship to Christ.

The “middle wall of partition” is a vivid architectural metaphor. A literal stone barrier in the Jerusalem temple courts separated the area open to Gentiles from the inner precincts reserved for Jews, and inscriptions warned Gentiles against crossing it. Paul’s wording may evoke that arrangement, though the explanation in verse 15 points beyond a particular wall to the covenantal regulations and social hostility that kept the two communities apart.

The barrier had also functioned as a fence around Israel, preserving a distinct people amid idolatrous nations. The divine purpose of Israel’s separation was not evil. Human sin, however, turned distinction into contempt and privilege into exclusion. What had served a temporary role in salvation history became an instrument of enmity.

Christ broke the wall down “in his flesh”—through His bodily death. He did not produce peace by declaring that sin and holiness no longer matter. The cross dealt with the sin that alienated both groups from God, removing every basis for spiritual boasting.

Church unity therefore cannot be reduced to friendliness. Christ Himself is its foundation and content. Whenever race, nationality, caste, class, language, or inherited tradition is made a condition of full fellowship, believers begin rebuilding what the crucified Lord destroyed. The church becomes visibly Christian when people formerly separated discover that Christ is sufficient to make them one.

wordNotes.term: he is our peace — αὐτός ἐστιν ἡ εἰρήνη ἡμῶν (autos estin hē eirēnē hēmōn)
wordNotes.explanation: Christ does more than announce or negotiate peace. In His person and saving work He embodies the reconciliation that unites believers to God and to one another.

wordNotes.term: middle wall of partition — τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ (to mesotoichon tou phragmou)
wordNotes.explanation: The architectural image describes a separating wall or enclosing fence. It represents the covenantal and social barriers that divided Jews and Gentiles and produced hostility between them.

verses.bibleText: Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The means by which Christ broke the dividing wall is now explained. He acted “in his flesh,” referring to His bodily sacrifice on the cross. His true humanity matters: reconciliation was accomplished through an actual life offered and an actual death endured. Yet the One who gave that life is the divine Son, making His self-offering sufficient for all who come to God through Him.

Paul says Christ abolished “the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances.” The expression has generated substantial debate. The wording may encompass the Mosaic legal order as a covenantal administration, but the immediate concern is its role as a boundary and source of condemnation. Circumcision, sacrifices, ritual purity rules, festivals, and other ceremonial or boundary-marking decrees distinguished Israel from the nations. Once their typological purpose was fulfilled in Christ, they could no longer serve as conditions of access to God or membership in His people.

The cross therefore brought the ceremonial economy to its appointed fulfilment. Sacrifices and sanctuary rites had pointed forward to Christ; when the true sacrifice was offered, the shadows no longer governed covenant life. Gentiles did not need to pass through that system in order to reach the Messiah. This does not erase every biblical teaching related to food. The clean-and-unclean distinction predates Sinai, and Scripture’s call to honor God with the body remains relevant; neither principle functions as a means of justification or a test of ethnic access to Christ.

The wording does not teach that God’s moral character or moral law was abolished. Later in the same letter Paul quotes the fifth commandment as authoritative Christian instruction. Elsewhere he says that faith establishes the law and that the Spirit enables its righteous requirement to be fulfilled in believers. Under the new covenant, God writes His law upon the heart. Christ abolished enmity, condemnation, and the former covenantal barrier—not holiness, love, or obedience.

Even where the phrase is understood broadly as the Mosaic law in its former jurisdiction over Israel, its moral principles remain authoritative Scripture as interpreted through Christ and embodied in the law of love. The believer obeys God’s commandments not as a means of earning justification but as the fruit of new-covenant life. Nothing in this passage transfers sacredness from the seventh-day Sabbath to Sunday or supplies any basis for such a change.

Christ’s purpose was “to make in himself of twain one new man.” He did not declare one group victorious over the other. Nor did He merely negotiate peaceful coexistence between unchanged identities. He performed an act of creation. Jews and Gentiles who believe become one new humanity because both die to their former boasting and receive a common life in Him.

“New” signifies more than recent. This community belongs to the new creation inaugurated by Christ’s resurrection. Its members retain personal and cultural distinctiveness, but no distinction grants superiority or excludes another believer from full fellowship.

Peace is therefore both accomplished and assigned. Christ has made peace objectively at the cross; His people must now live according to what He created. Whenever ceremonial preferences, cultural customs, or human regulations are elevated into saving requirements, the old wall begins to rise again. Faithfulness to Christ means refusing both lawlessness and legalism—receiving righteousness as a gift and walking in the obedience that grace produces.

wordNotes.term: law of commandments contained in ordinances — τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν (ton nomon tōn entolōn en dogmasin)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes the Mosaic legal order expressed in authoritative decrees. In this context the focus falls especially on the ceremonial, ritual, and boundary-setting requirements that distinguished Israel from the Gentiles and had become a dividing barrier.

wordNotes.term: one new man — εἷς καινὸς ἄνθρωπος (heis kainos anthrōpos)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression means one new humanity. Christ does not merely place two unreconciled groups beside one another; He creates a new corporate people whose defining identity is found in Him.

verses.bibleText: And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The new humanity exists because both groups have been reconciled to God. Horizontal peace cannot be separated from vertical reconciliation. Human hostility grows from a deeper alienation from the Creator, and lasting unity becomes possible only as that alienation is healed.

“Both” means Jew and Gentile. Israel’s historical nearness did not remove the need for reconciliation. Possession of Scripture, covenant signs, and religious heritage could not atone for sin. The Gentile who was far and the Jew who was near must both come through the same cross.

They are reconciled “in one body.” The body is primarily the unified church described in verses 15 and 18. God does not save isolated individuals while leaving them free to preserve structures of contempt. He incorporates them into a people whose common life announces that the old hostility has been judged.

The means is “the cross.” Christ’s death was not merely an example of courageous love, though it reveals love perfectly. He bore sin, met its condemnation, and offered Himself once for all. Reconciliation is possible because the objective cause of estrangement has been dealt with, not because God simply ignores rebellion.

Paul’s phrase “having slain the enmity thereby” is deliberately forceful. At the place where Christ was killed, enmity itself received its deathblow. The cross exposes the murderous character of human hostility while absorbing and overcoming it through self-giving love.

This reconciliation is sufficient for all but is not imposed irrespective of faith. Verse 8 has already identified faith as the means by which salvation is received. Those who remain outside Christ remain unreconciled in experience, even though the gospel invitation is genuinely extended to them.

The church is meant to be the visible social form of reconciliation. Unity does not require silence about injustice or the erasure of truth. The cross brings sin into judgment and forgives the repentant; Christian reconciliation must follow the same pattern of truth, repentance, grace, and restored fellowship.

A congregation divided by ethnic pride or social exclusion contradicts the one body created by Christ. Believers do not create unity through human diplomacy, but they are responsible to preserve and embody the unity for which their Lord died.

wordNotes.explanation: The intensified verb describes the restoration of a broken relationship. Through Christ’s death, believing Jews and Gentiles are brought from hostility into peace with God.

wordNotes.term: in one body — ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι (en heni sōmati)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase refers primarily to the one church created from Jewish and Gentile believers. Their reconciliation with God is experienced within a community already reconciled across ethnic boundaries.

verses.bibleText: And came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The crucified and risen Christ is also the herald of the peace He accomplished. The language echoes Isaiah’s announcement of good news and the promise of “peace” to those who were far and near. What the prophets anticipated has arrived through Jesus.

During His earthly ministry Christ proclaimed the kingdom and called sinners into reconciliation with God. His immediate work was concentrated among Israel, yet after His resurrection He commissioned the gospel to all nations. He therefore “came and preached” to Gentiles through the apostles and other Spirit-empowered messengers. When the true gospel is proclaimed, the risen Lord addresses hearers through His Word.

Peace is announced “to you which were afar off,” the Gentiles described in verses 11–13. They are not offered a lesser place or a delayed fellowship. The same message is also preached “to them that were nigh.” Jewish privilege did not eliminate the need for the gospel. Nearness to covenant revelation is not identical with reconciliation to God.

The repetition of peace gives equal dignity and equal need to both groups. Gentiles must not despise the people through whom the promises came, and Jews must not treat Gentile believers as secondary recipients. Both hear the same Christ announce the same peace secured by the same cross.

Christian proclamation must therefore match its content. A message of peace delivered in arrogance, racial superiority, or contempt contradicts the One whose gospel is being spoken. Christ’s ambassadors announce not the triumph of one human culture over another but the reign of the Lord who reconciles enemies to God and makes them one.

wordNotes.explanation: The expression means that Christ announced the good news of peace. He proclaimed it in His earthly ministry and continued to speak through the Spirit-empowered witness of His apostles and church.

verses.bibleText: For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peace is proved by access. Through Christ, “we both”—Jewish and Gentile believers—may approach the Father in one Spirit. The verse gathers the work of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit into one saving movement: through the Son, in the Spirit, unto the Father.

Access was a serious matter in the ancient world. Ordinary people did not freely enter the presence of a king, and Israel’s sanctuary taught that sinful humanity cannot casually enter the holy presence of God. Approach required divine provision, sacrifice, priesthood, and cleansing.

Christ has supplied that provision. His sacrifice was offered once for all, and the risen Son remains the living mediator through whom believers draw near. Access through Him does not bypass His priestly ministry; it depends upon it. Because He intercedes in the heavenly sanctuary, believers may come boldly to the throne of grace for mercy and help.

The Father is the destination of this approach. Reconciliation does not lead into an impersonal sacred force but into family fellowship. Those once described as children of wrath are welcomed to the Father through the beloved Son.

The Spirit makes the access a living experience. He awakens faith, assures believers of adoption, shapes prayer, and unites worshippers who once stood apart. “One Spirit” excludes the notion that Jewish and Gentile Christians possess separate spiritual paths. Their experiences and cultures may differ, but the life animating them is one.

This access is present and continuing. It is not the claim that believers have already undergone bodily translation to heaven. They approach God through faith and prayer while living on earth, and they await the resurrection and visible presence of God in the new creation.

No ethnic gatekeeper, human priestly caste, or personal achievement can add to what Christ provides. Ministers may teach and serve, but they cannot become alternative mediators of saving access. Every believer comes through the same Son and in the same Spirit.

The privilege carries an ethical demand. People who approach one Father through one Christ cannot defend contempt for one another. Shared worship should train the church to recognise a shared family identity stronger than the divisions of the former life.

wordNotes.explanation: The word conveys introduction or approach into the presence of another. Through Christ, believers are brought confidently before God, who is here revealed as their Father.

wordNotes.term: by one Spirit — ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι (en heni pneumati)
wordNotes.explanation: Jewish and Gentile believers approach God in the shared life and unity created by the one Holy Spirit. The Spirit applies Christ’s work and forms worshippers into one people.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The conclusion begins with civic language familiar in the Greco-Roman world. Cities distinguished full citizens from resident aliens and temporary foreigners. Rights, protection, social honour, and participation varied according to status. Paul declares that Gentile believers no longer occupy the margins of God’s people.

They are “fellowcitizens with the saints.” The saints are not a spiritual aristocracy or a small class recognised after death. They are all whom God has set apart in Christ. Gentile Christians possess the same citizenship as Jewish Christians and every other believer. There are no probationary citizens in the kingdom of grace.

Citizenship then deepens into family: they belong to “the household of God.” A government may grant legal standing while remaining personally distant; a household implies belonging, care, inheritance, discipline, and shared life. The God approached as Father in verse 18 receives the reconciled as family members.

This new identity does not erase earthly responsibilities. Christians may belong to different nations and cultures, but no political loyalty can become more ultimate than membership in God’s household. When national, racial, caste, or class allegiance demands contempt for fellow believers, the household of God must govern the Christian conscience.

Family belonging also creates obligations. Members do not merely claim privileges from the Father; they learn to bear one another’s burdens, speak truth, forgive, serve, and preserve unity. A church that treats some believers as permanent guests has failed to live according to the status Christ has granted them.

The movement from stranger to citizen and family member answers the losses of verse 12. Those once alienated from Israel’s community now share the life of all God’s saints. Those once without God now live in His own household. Grace has not merely shortened the distance; it has changed outsiders into sons and daughters.

wordNotes.term: strangers and foreigners — ξένοι καὶ πάροικοι (xenoi kai paroikoi)
wordNotes.explanation: The terms describe outsiders and resident aliens who lacked the full rights of citizens. Paul uses them metaphorically to contrast the Gentiles’ former exclusion with their complete membership in God’s people.

wordNotes.term: household of God — οἰκεῖοι τοῦ θεοῦ (oikeioi tou theou)
wordNotes.explanation: Believers are not merely citizens under God’s rule but members of His family. The expression prepares for the building and temple imagery of verses 20–22.

verses.bibleText: And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The household becomes a building, and the security of Gentile inclusion is traced to its foundation. They have not entered a temporary religious experiment. God has incorporated them into a structure grounded in His authoritative revelation of Christ.

The “apostles and prophets” are likely the foundational messengers of the apostolic age, the same groups joined in Ephesians 3:5 and distinguished among Christ’s gifts in Ephesians 4:11. The apostles bore authorised witness to the risen Lord and carried His gospel into the world. Prophets, directed by the Spirit, declared God’s message and helped guide the early church.

Calling them a foundation does not make their personalities the object of faith. Their foundational role lies in the gospel they received, proclaimed, and embodied. That testimony is preserved for the church in Scripture. Later generations do not lay a different foundation or create new revelation that overturns the apostolic gospel; they build upon what God established through those first witnesses.

Jesus Christ Himself is the “chief corner stone.” Paul distinguishes Him from every human messenger. Apostles and prophets serve within the building, but Christ gives the foundation its meaning and the whole structure its alignment.

The word may describe a stone placed at a foundational corner, setting the lines along which the walls were built. Some have understood it as an elevated finishing stone. The metaphor need not be pressed into only one architectural detail. Christ both grounds the church and governs its completion. Everything is measured by Him.

The language recalls Isaiah’s promise that God would lay a tested and precious stone in Zion. Jesus is dependable under the full weight of God’s saving purpose. Churches become unstable when they align themselves primarily with personalities, traditions, political movements, or cultural approval. Stability returns as doctrine, worship, ethics, and mission are brought back to Christ.

The cornerstone also joins walls approaching from different directions. Jewish and Gentile believers can meet without losing truth because both are aligned to the same Lord. Unity produced by ignoring Christ will eventually fracture; unity built around Him possesses divine coherence.

wordNotes.term: foundation of the apostles and prophets — θεμελίῳ τῶν ἀποστόλων καὶ προφητῶν (themeliō tōn apostolōn kai prophētōn)
wordNotes.explanation: The apostles and prophets form the foundation as the first Spirit-guided witnesses and proclaimers of Christ. The reference likely includes New Testament prophets associated with the apostolic mission.

The rare architectural term denotes a decisive corner stone that gives alignment, stability, and unity to the building. Whether pictured low in the foundation or as the crowning stone, Christ governs the whole structure.

verses.bibleText: In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The building is neither static nor loosely assembled. In Christ, “all the building fitly framed together groweth.” Paul combines architectural and organic imagery: the church is under construction, yet it grows like a living body.

Every part is joined “in whom”—in Christ. He is not only the cornerstone laid at the beginning; He remains the sphere and source of continuing growth. Separation from Him cannot be compensated for by organizational efficiency or religious activity.

“Fitly framed together” pictures stones carefully shaped and placed in relation to one another. Believers are not gathered as an unrelated crowd. God gives gifts, relationships, responsibilities, and opportunities through which each contributes to the whole. Diversity is retained, but isolation and rivalry contradict the design.

The destination is “an holy temple in the Lord.” In Roman Asia, magnificent temples dominated public life, and Ephesus was renowned for the temple of Artemis. Paul identifies the true dwelling associated with the living God not with an impressive pagan sanctuary, nor ultimately with a building made by human hands, but with a people reconciled in Christ.

The imagery also fulfils the scriptural hope that the nations would be welcomed into the worship of God. Gentile believers are not confined to an outer court. Together with Jewish believers, they constitute the temple itself.

Holiness is essential to the metaphor. God’s temple is set apart for His presence and purpose. Unity cannot be maintained by treating sin as harmless. The same grace that reconciles also cleanses, disciplines, and transforms. A holy church is not a community boasting of moral superiority, but one continually yielding to the sanctifying work of the Spirit.

The present tense “groweth” keeps the church humble. God’s work is real but unfinished. Individual believers and congregations still require correction, maturity, and deeper union. The final beauty of the temple will appear only when Christ completes His people.

No stone grows alone. Christian maturity is corporate as well as personal. Patience, forgiveness, truth, service, and mutual submission are among the means by which believers remain fitted together while God’s temple rises.

wordNotes.explanation: The architectural term describes parts being carefully fitted and joined. Unity is not accidental proximity; Christ places diverse believers into a coherent structure.
Naos commonly refers to the sanctuary or temple proper. The reconciled community becomes the sacred dwelling associated with God’s presence, not merely an outer gathering around holy things.

verses.bibleText: In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul turns the temple image directly toward his Gentile readers: “ye also.” They must never imagine that the preceding promises belong chiefly to Jewish Christians while they occupy an attached but inferior structure. God is building them into the same dwelling.

The present passive form, “are builded together,” portrays an ongoing divine work. God is the Builder, Christ is the cornerstone and sphere of construction, and believers are joined together by the Spirit. The church is both already God’s dwelling and still being formed into what He intends.

The prefix translated “together” carries the burden of the paragraph. Gentiles are built with Jews, former strangers with covenant heirs, and people from divided cultures with one another. A collection of segregated communities may use Christian language, but it falls short of the architecture displayed here.

The goal is “an habitation of God.” The Creator who cannot be contained by temples chooses to make His covenant presence known within a reconciled people. This presence is not controlled by architecture, wealth, institutional prestige, or human ritual. It is given “through the Spirit.”

The corporate emphasis complements, rather than denies, the Spirit’s indwelling of individual believers. Each Christian belongs to God bodily and personally, yet Paul’s concern here is the assembled community. Qualities that cannot be practised alone—love, patience, forgiveness, unity, burden-bearing—become visible evidence that the Spirit inhabits the church.

The temple metaphor should not be confused with a denial of the real heavenly sanctuary. The New Testament can describe God’s people as His spiritual temple while also presenting Christ as minister in the true sanctuary above. Here the emphasis is earthly and corporate: through the Spirit, God makes His reconciled people a living witness to His presence, while Christ’s heavenly ministry remains the ground of their access and hope.

This indwelling anticipates the final promise of Scripture: God will dwell with redeemed humanity in the renewed creation. The church now offers a partial and imperfect foretaste of that future. Wherever Christ joins former enemies, the Spirit produces holiness, and the Father is worshipped as the common Father of all, the coming dwelling of God with humanity is already being announced.

wordNotes.explanation: The present passive form indicates an ongoing work God performs upon the community. Gentile believers are being built together with all other believers, not formed into a separate spiritual structure.

wordNotes.term: habitation of God — κατοικητήριον τοῦ θεοῦ (katoikētērion tou theou)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes a settled dwelling place. Through the Holy Spirit, God makes the reconciled community the sphere of His covenant presence.
